title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
spaceBreakdown:
- only fixed int variables lo, hi, mid → O(1)
- no containers, no recursion → O(1)
- not counted: input vector
approach: Use binary search comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`. If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the minimum must be in the right half (set `lo = mid+1`). If `nums[mid] < nums[hi]`, the minimum is in the left half including `mid` (set `hi = mid`). When they are equal, duplicates make the side ambiguous, so safely shrink the range by `hi--`. This preserves the minimum because `nums[hi]` has an equal copy still in range. Worst case (all duplicates) degrades to O(n); average is O(log n).
hints:
Compare the middle element to the last element of the current range - what does their order tell you about which half contains the rotation point (and thus the minimum)?
The array was sorted in ascending order before being rotated between 1 and n times.
Binary search on the index range. In `[2,2,2,0,1]`, mid index 2 has value 2 and nums[hi]=1; since 2 > 1, the minimum is to the right, so move lo to mid+1.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
    if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
    else if nums[mid] < nums[hi]: hi = mid
    else: hi = hi - 1
return nums[lo]

**Single element** - n = 1, loop never runs.
`Input: [1]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: returning `nums[lo+1]` or accessing `nums[mid]` before checking `lo < hi` → out-of-bounds / wrong value.

**All duplicates** - every element equal, so comparisons never disambiguate a side.
`Input: [2,2,2,2]` → `Expected: 2`
⚠️ Bug: using `hi = mid` in the equal case (instead of `hi--`) → infinite loop on `[2,2,2,2]` because lo=0, hi=3, mid=1 keeps setting hi=1, then mid=0 sets hi=0 only after several steps but can stall on ranges like `[2,2]` where mid=0 and hi=1 with equal values loops forever if you do `hi = mid`.

**Min at boundary** - minimum is the last element.
`Input: [3,3,1,3]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[lo]` instead of `nums[hi]` → returns 3, because `nums[mid] >= nums[lo]` looks "sorted" and wrongly keeps the right half.

**Min at first position** - already sorted, no real rotation effect.
`Input: [1,2,3,4,5]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: always doing `lo = mid + 1` when `nums[mid] == nums[hi]` → skips index 0 and returns 2.

**Three elements with wraparound** - small range where mid equals lo.
`Input: [3,1,3]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: using `mid = (lo + hi + 1) / 2` (upper mid) → on `[3,1,3]` with lo=0, hi=2 gives mid=1 (ok here), but on `[2,2]` gives mid=1 and `hi = mid` stalls forever.

followUps.q: What if the array has no duplicates - can you guarantee O(log n)?
followUps.a: Yes. Without duplicates the `nums[mid] == nums[hi]` branch never triggers, so each step halves the range. Time becomes O(log n), space stays O(1).

followUps.q: What if you must also return the index of the minimum (the rotation count)?
followUps.a: Return `lo` instead of `nums[lo]` after the same loop. The invariant `nums[lo]` is the minimum still holds, and `lo` is exactly the rotation offset. Time O(n) worst case, space O(1).

followUps.q: What if the array is too large to fit in memory and arrives as a stream with random access via an API `get(i)`?
followUps.a: Run the same binary search using `get(i)` calls; the equal-case `hi--` still works but may issue up to O(n) calls in the all-duplicate case. If duplicates are rare, expected calls are O(log n); space remains O(1) since no buffering is needed.
